Thanks for the time earlier today — good conversation. Quick write-up to capture what we discussed, proposed next steps, and a few technical clarifications the engineering team asked us to confirm. Attaching a one-page integration checklist and a draft SOW for your procurement team.

Summary (from call):
- Use case: real-time search augmentation + nearline batch embeddings for analytic pipelines.
- Priority: low-latency retrieval for UI (sub-200ms median) & high-throughput batch embedding for nightly jobs.
- Concern: how Redwood rate limits/quotas will interact with our ingestion pipeline and retries (429s).

Action items / next steps:
1) Tech deep-dive: schedule 60m SRE/architect call with your cloud infra team to walk SDK auth, routing, and recommended retry/idempotency patterns (Dev to lead).
2) Integration checklist: please review attached "redwood-integration-checklist.pdf" and highlight any missing infra constraints.
3) Procurement: review attached SOW; Marissa will follow up with updated pricing and any procurement questions.

Technical clarifications we promised to follow up on (short answers below; Dev will send a detailed note):
- SDK setup & auth: Redwood SDK supports API keys and ephemeral tokens (short-lived) via our auth service. For production we recommend using ephemeral tokens minted by your service account (good for least privilege).
- Routing / regional endpoints: We can pin requests to region-specific endpoints to keep traffic in-region. SDK has a region config param.
- Structured output & tool-calling: Our chat + structured output supports schema enforcement and function/tool-calls. You can declare tool signatures; the runtime will enforce typed outputs and route tool calls to your service via Webhook.
- Embeddings & rerankers: For real-time retrieval we recommend embedding + ANN index (your side) and call our reranker endpoint for second-stage scoring when context is large. Batch embeddings should be grouped into bulk upsert calls (we support upsert endpoints with deterministic IDs).
- Rate limiting & retries: Default hosted quotas are per-account and per-route. We heard that you need clear guidance on 429 handling, idempotency, and backoff strategies — asking Dev to provide a prescriptive pattern (headers to set, backoff timings, request IDs).

Please confirm the names/roles who should join the SRE deep-dive next week and a couple of time windows that work for you.

Thanks,

Hi Mike — quick technical follow-up with recommended, production-ready patterns you can adopt today. Long-form reference follows; happy to walk through on the SRE call.

1) SDK setup & auth
- Recommended pattern: your service should mint short-lived ephemeral tokens (valid ~5–15 minutes) for end-user requests. Use a backend service account with a long-lived API key only for token minting.
- SDK config example (pseudocode):
  - client = RedwoodClient(apiKey=EPHEMERAL_TOKEN, region="us-west-2", timeout=30s)

2) Routing & regional endpoints
- Configure per-route routing if you want to separate UI traffic (low-latency) from batch traffic (throughput). We can supply multiple endpoints and a routing policy:
  - ui.redwood.api (low-latency SLOs)
  - batch.redwood.api (high-throughput, higher cost-efficiency)

3) Embeddings & reranker workflow
- Batch ingestion: create deterministic IDs (e.g., sha256(namespace||doc_id)) and call embeddings.upsert(batch) with 512-2048 batch size (tune to your memory footprint). Use upsert idempotency (see below) to avoid duplicates.
- Real-time retrieval: compute embedding for query -> ANN lookup -> optionally call reranker.score(batch of candidates) for top-N re-ranking. Reranker accepts both embeddings and text context.

4) Idempotency, request IDs, and dedupe
- Set X-Request-ID for every client request; set Idempotency-Key (or Idempotency-Request) for non-idempotent endpoints you intend to retry (upsert, create-session). The server will return 409 if an idempotency conflict occurs.
- For bulk upserts, use deterministic IDs to make operations naturally idempotent (upsert semantics).

5) Rate limiting & 429 handling (prescriptive)
- Quotas: hosted accounts have per-minute token quotas and per-route concurrency limits. Dedicated customers can reserve capacity with predictable throughput.
- Retry guidance (recommended):
  - On 429 with Retry-After header: honor Retry-After if present.
  - If no Retry-After header: use exponential backoff with full jitter. Suggested parameters: initial=200ms, multiplier=2, max=10s, attempts=6.
  - Pseudocode backoff with full jitter:
    delay = random_between(0, min(max_delay, base * 2**attempt))

- Idempotency + Retries: when retries are used, ensure Idempotency-Key is sent for requests that mutate state. For read-only generation calls that can safely be retried, X-Request-ID is enough for tracing.

6) Concurrency & batching knobs
- For embeddings ingestion: parallelize across workers, but limit concurrent upsert calls to ~4–8 per worker depending on batch size and your bandwidth. Monitor 429s and lower concurrency if you see spikes.
- For streaming generation to UI: prefer single open stream per end-user request and avoid retrying streams; if a stream fails early, fall back to a non-streaming re-request with the same X-Request-ID so you can correlate logs.

7) Observability & tracing
- Always set X-Request-ID and pass it through your logs and incident traces. We surface our server-side request-id in the response header (Redwood-Server-Request-Id) for cross-correlation.

Attachments: I attached our lightweight integration checklist (Ben included) and a one-page retry/backoff cheatsheet you can use in your SDK wrappers.

If helpful I can drop minimal client code for generating Idempotency-Key + exponential backoff wrapper in Node/python on the call.
